# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of ischemic stroke, accounting for a substantial proportion of cardioembolic events [1]. Oral anticoagulation (OAC) with vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) remains the cornerstone of stroke prevention in patients with non-valvular AF [2]. However, a considerable subset of patients cannot tolerate long-term anticoagulation owing to bleeding risk or contraindications [3]. Given that the left atrial appendage (LAA) is the source of more than 90% of thrombi in non-valvular AF, percutaneous LAA closure (LAAC) has emerged as a mechanical alternative for stroke prevention [4].

## Rationale and Anatomy

The LAA is a trabeculated, blind-ended structure with highly variable morphology, commonly classified as "chicken wing," "windsock," "cactus," and "cauliflower" types [5]. Stasis within the appendage, particularly during AF, predisposes to thrombus formation [4]. Surgical exclusion of the LAA was historically performed during cardiac surgery, but incomplete closure was frequent [6]. Percutaneous techniques were developed to provide reliable, catheter-based exclusion without the morbidity of surgery [7].

## Devices and Technique

The two most widely studied endocardial occluders are the Watchman device (Boston Scientific) and the Amplatzer Amulet (Abbott) [8,9]. The procedure is performed via transseptal puncture under fluoroscopic and transesophageal echocardiographic (TEE) guidance, with increasing use of intracardiac echocardiography [10]. Accurate sizing using preprocedural imaging, including cardiac computed tomography, optimizes device selection and reduces complications [11]. The epicardial LARIAT system offers an alternative ligation approach but is less commonly used [12].

## Pivotal Clinical Evidence

The PROTECT AF trial first demonstrated that the Watchman device was non-inferior to warfarin for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death in patients eligible for anticoagulation [13]. The subsequent PREVAIL trial addressed procedural safety concerns and contributed to regulatory approval [14]. A patient-level meta-analysis of PROTECT AF and PREVAIL with extended follow-up confirmed comparable stroke prevention and significant reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and cardiovascular mortality [15]. Long-term five-year outcomes of PROTECT AF reinforced these findings [16].

For patients with contraindications to anticoagulation, the ASAP study showed acceptable event rates with single antiplatelet therapy or aspirin alone following Watchman implantation [17]. The PRAGUE-17 trial compared LAAC with DOACs in high-risk patients and demonstrated non-inferiority for major cardiovascular and bleeding events [18]. The Amulet IDE trial directly compared the Amplatzer Amulet with the Watchman, showing comparable efficacy with differing complication profiles [19].

## Registry and Real-World Data

Large registries have provided valuable real-world insights. The EWOLUTION registry demonstrated high implantation success and low periprocedural complication rates in routine practice [20]. The National Cardiovascular Data Registry LAAO Registry, encompassing tens of thousands of US procedures, confirmed favorable contemporary safety outcomes [21]. The Amulet observational registry similarly reported high closure rates across diverse anatomies [22].

## Complications and Device-Related Concerns

Procedural complications include pericardial effusion and tamponade, device embolization, and vascular access complications [23]. Device-related thrombus (DRT) is an important late concern, occurring in approximately 3–4% of patients and associated with increased thromboembolic risk [24]. Peridevice leak, identified on follow-up imaging, has also been linked to adverse outcomes, though its clinical significance varies [25]. Optimal antithrombotic regimens after implantation remain debated, with strategies ranging from short-course DOACs to dual antiplatelet therapy [26].

## Current Guidelines and Patient Selection

Current guidelines assign LAAC a role primarily in patients with non-valvular AF at elevated stroke risk who have contraindications to long-term anticoagulation [2,27]. Shared decision-making is emphasized, given the procedural risks and the relative paucity of head-to-head data against DOACs [27]. Appropriate patient selection, integrating stroke and bleeding risk scores, is essential to maximize net clinical benefit [28].

## Future Directions

Ongoing randomized trials, including CHAMPION-AF and OPTION, are evaluating LAAC against DOACs in broader populations and in combination with ablation [29]. Refinements in device design, imaging-guided sizing, and antithrombotic protocols aim to reduce DRT and peridevice leak [30]. The combination of LAAC with catheter ablation in a single procedure represents an evolving strategy warranting further study [29].

## Conclusion

Percutaneous LAAC has become an established option for stroke prevention in selected patients with non-valvular AF, particularly those unsuitable for long-term anticoagulation. Robust randomized and registry data support its efficacy and safety, although questions regarding optimal device selection, antithrombotic management, and comparative effectiveness against DOACs remain. Forthcoming trials will help define the future role of LAAC across the AF population.
